title: Pongal / Onam (regional; harvest)
hook: a flower carpet that grows every morning for ten days, because a beloved king is coming home to check on his people

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pongal: a new pot boiling over in the sun, and four days of thank-yous, cattle included. Your line was more than the pot can hold. Today, the other harvest, in Kerala, and a look back at the week.
screen: `PONGAL: MORE THAN THE POT CAN HOLD.`

segments.voice: In Kerala, in late summer, on the first morning of Onam, someone gets up early and lays a small circle of flower petals at the front door. Yellow, orange, white. Next morning, it grows a ring. And the next. For ten days it grows, a carpet of flowers called a pookalam, until by the last day it's a whole bright mandala across the doorstep. Why the trouble? A guest is coming. Not a god this time. A king, and he wants to see that his people are happy.
screen: `A CIRCLE OF PETALS AT THE DOOR.` → `BIGGER EVERY MORNING FOR TEN DAYS.` → `A KING IS COMING.`

segments.voice: The king is Mahabali, an asura, from the side of the story usually cast as the gods' rivals. But in Kerala he's remembered as the best king there ever was. A Malayalam folk song still sung at Onam remembers his reign as a time when all people were equal: no lies, no cheating, no one poor. The gods grew worried about how powerful he'd become. So Vishnu came to him as Vamana, a small boy-priest, and asked for just as much land as he could cover in three steps. Bali, who never refused anyone, said yes. And the boy grew. One step covered the earth. The second, the heavens. There was nowhere left for the third, so Bali bowed and offered his own head. Vamana's foot pressed him down into the world below. The Bhagavata Purana tells it as a story of Bali's devotion and generosity: he's rewarded, not destroyed. Kerala adds something: Bali asked to visit his people once a year. Onam is that visit, so everyone makes sure he'll find them well. The pookalam. New clothes. The Onam sadhya, a huge vegetarian feast on a banana leaf, often more than twenty dishes, eaten together. Boat races on the backwaters. It's Kerala's harvest festival too, in the month of Chingam. And that's the week: Shivaratri's four watches and its pillar of light, Raksha Bandhan's thread, the sun turning at Sankranti, Pongal's pot, and a king coming home. Different stories, same instinct: make the day worth arriving for.
screen: `AN ASURA, THE BEST OF KINGS.` · `THREE STEPS: EARTH, HEAVEN, HIS HEAD.` · `ONE VISIT A YEAR: ONAM.` · `THE WEEK: VIGIL, THREAD, SUN, POT.` · then, large: `MAKE THE DAY WORTH ARRIVING FOR.`

segments.voice: Imagine Mahabali is visiting you this year, not to judge, just to see how you are. For each thing that's good in your life right now, lay one ring of petals at your door, and let the circle grow without rushing it. When it's full, sit beside it like someone waiting for a guest they love.
Pongal and Onam. Two harvests: Tamil Nadu's pot boiling over for the sun, and Kerala's flower carpet for a king who comes home once a year.
Your line: worth arriving for. A week of festivals, behind you. That's day one hundred fifty-four.
